en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Retribution of Sin and Merit, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Khotan during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at the Śākya Monastery in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, together with...
Accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
when the nine-month retreat had concluded at one time, he emerged from the divine chamber and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Between the two countries stands a great tree named Nyagrodha, twenty *li* in height, with branches spreading out in a square and circular canopy covering sixty *li*.
Upon this tree are tens of millions of *hu* of fruit; when eaten, they are fragrant and sweet, their flavor like honey.
Sweet fruits ripened and fell for the people to eat; all their ailments were eliminated, and their eyes became clear and sharp.
The Buddha sat beneath the tree, and at that time, the bhikṣus gathered the fruits and ate them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I observe that among the heavens, the earth, and all things, each has its own past affinity.
Ānanda immediately stepped forward, prostrated himself before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"What were their past conditions?
These disciples wish to hear of them.
Please explain them fully, so as to enlighten those who have not yet heard."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Excellent, excellent!
If you wish to hear it, listen with a single-minded focus."
The Buddha said:
"When a person creates merit, it is like this tree: originally planted from a single seed, it gradually grows until its benefit is limitless.
Those who become noble, wealthy, kings, or elders have come from having honored and served the Triple Gem."
One will become a person of great wealth with limitless possessions,
arising from the practice of giving;
one will be long-lived, free from illness, and possess a robust physique.
They come from upholding the precepts;

they are upright in appearance, with a complexion as pure and radiant as the finest countenance, hands and body soft and supple, and breath fragrant and clean; all who behold their features rejoice and never tire of gazing upon them—this comes from patience;
they are diligent in cultivation without indolence and delight in performing meritorious deeds—this comes from vigor.
He is composed and serene, his speech and conduct are deliberate and precise, having emerged from meditative concentration;

he is exceptionally intelligent and proficient, understanding profound dharmas, expounding sublime meanings to enlighten the ignorant and deluded; when people hear his words, there are none who do not consult him, receive his teachings, and apply them as treasures, for he has emerged from wisdom;
his voice is clear and penetrating, having emerged from chanting praises to the Triple Gem.
One is pure and free from disease because one has come from a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and did not inflict blows or punishments in previous lives.
One is tall and handsome because one showed respect to others;
one is short and small because one treated others with contempt.
One is ugly because one delights in anger;
one is born ignorant because one does not study;
one is dull-witted because one does not teach others.
One becomes mute and speech-impaired because of slandering and毁毀 (ruining) others;
one becomes deaf and blind because of not beholding the sutras and dharmas and not hearing the sutras;
one becomes a slave because of failing to repay debts.
One becomes lowly and base because one failed to pay respect to the Triple Gem;
one becomes ugly and dark-complexioned because one obstructed the light before the Buddha;
one is born in a land of the naked because one treated the Buddha’s vihāra with careless disregard while wearing light clothing.
One is born in the land of the Horse-Hoofed People because one wore wooden clogs while treading before the Buddha;
one is born in the land of the Chest-Pierced People because one gave alms to cultivate merit with a mind of regret and attachment;
and one is born among the deer, roe deer, elk, and antelope because one delighted in frightening people.
One is born among the dragons because one delighted in frivolous play;
one’s body develops malignant sores that are difficult to treat and heal because one delighted in whipping and beating sentient beings;
and people see one with joy because in previous lives one saw others with delight.
If people see him and are not pleased, it is because in a previous life he saw others with displeasure;
if he delights in encountering officials who imprison him in jail and bind his body with shackles and clogs, it is because in a previous life he confined sentient beings in cages against their will;
if his lips are cleft, it is because in a previous life he caught fish by piercing their mouths with hooks.

If one hears pleasant words and virtuous speech yet finds no joy in hearing them, and amidst such clamor makes noise that disturbs others from listening to and receiving the Dharma, they will later be reborn as a dog with drooping ears.
If one hears the discourse on the Dharma yet does not take it to heart or absorb it, they will later be reborn among long-eared donkeys and horses.
Those who are stingy and greedy, eating alone, fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*);
when reborn as humans, they are poor and famished, with clothing that cannot even cover their bodies.
Those who eat the fine things themselves while giving the coarse things to others later fall among pigs, swine, and dung beetles.
Those who plunder the property or persons of others will later fall among sheep, where people will flay their skin alive.
Those who delight in killing living beings will later be born as floating insects upon the water, living in the morning and dying by evening.
Those who take pleasure in stealing the wealth and property of others will, in a future life, be reborn among cattle, horses, slaves, or servants to repay their past debts.
Those who take pleasure in violating the wives and daughters of others will, after death, enter hell; there the men shall embrace copper pillars and the women shall lie upon iron beds.
When they are reborn as humans, they fall among chickens and ducks.
Those who delight in speaking falsehoods and spreading evil about others will enter hell, where molten copper is poured into their mouths and their tongues are pulled out and plowed with oxen.

When they are reborn, they fall among the foul-sounding birds such as owls and magpies; whenever people hear their cries, they are all struck with terror and cry out that it is a portentous calamity, casting spells to bring about their death.
One who delights in drinking alcohol and becomes intoxicated commits thirty-six transgressions; after death, they fall into the *Kvathita-gūtha* (Boiling Excrement) hell;
when reborn, they fall among the *Śṛgāla* (Jackal) spirits;
and later, if born as a human, they will be foolish, dull-witted, and ignorant.
Those husband and wife who do not live in harmony and accord, frequently quarreling and mutually driving each other away, will later be reborn among pigeons and doves.
Those who covet the labor of others will later be reborn as elephants.

Those who serve as district magistrates or county governors and receive grain and food from the government, yet commit crimes or privately oppress the people—beating them with whips and canes, coercing them into forced labor, and leaving them with no recourse for their grievances—shall be shackled and imprisoned without leniency. Afterward, they fall into hell, where their spirits endure ten thousand agonies for billions of years.

Emerging from that retribution, they fall among water buffaloes; with their noses and mouths pierced, they are made to pull boats and drag carts, being struck and beaten with heavy clubs to repay their past offenses.
Those who do not practice self-restraint and purity come from among pigs.
Those who are stingy, greedy, and lack aspiration come from among dogs.
Those who are obstinate, perverse, and self-willed come from among sheep.
Those who are unsettled and unable to endure circumstances when among people come from among the monkeys.
Those whose human bodies are foul-smelling come from among the fish and turtles.
Those who are fierce and malevolent, harboring a poisonous heart, come from among the vipers.
Those who are fond of fine foods and kill sentient beings without a heart of compassion come from among jackals, wolves, cats, and hawks.

Their lives in this world are short; their pregnancies are harmed or result in miscarriages, and they die prematurely before long. They fall into the three miserable realms, where for tens of millions of kalpas there will be no end to their suffering.
“Be careful, be careful! The Buddha said, “In performing any meritorious deed, one should do it oneself.

When burning incense, offering food for merit, or reciting scriptures, one must not request others to do so without giving them a reward (dakṣiṇā). Is it possible that by hiring someone to eat, one can satisfy oneself while leaving the other hungry?”
By burning incense with purity, one attains *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom) and gathers all thoughts.
By lighting lamps with clarity, one obtains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) without obstruction.

Making it a constant practice to burn incense, eat pure food, recite sutras, and give alms, one gains merit through giving; the various devas will assist and protect one, while all manner of evils are repelled and all heterodox influences are overcome.
For those who are indolent, things appear peaceful and harmonious.

Lacking a mind of diligence, when suddenly afflicted by illness or encountering some inauspicious event, they then wish to burn incense and claim they are performing meritorious acts. Yet before the various devas have descended and while the hordes of Māras still stand before them, they attempt to provoke and disturb them with all manner of transformations and anomalies. For this reason, one must always be diligent.
"Sin and merit follow a person like a shadow follows a form. Planting seeds in the field of merit is like the *nyagrodha* tree: when first planting it, how many seeds were sown?
Ānanda knelt with palms joined and replied to the Buddha, "I planted but a single seed;
it gradually grew larger until it yielded fruits beyond measure."
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! To give to one and receive ten thousandfold in return— this statement is not false.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The wise person delights in giving; Heavenly beings shall support them.
By giving one, they obtain ten thousandfold; They dwell in peace and their lifespan is long."
"Today, by bestowing gifts upon virtuous people, their merit is immeasurable;
all shall attain the Way of the Buddha and deliver beings throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Ordinary people are ignorant of birth and death; with their physical eyes, they do not know of sin or merit.

I, by means of the eye of the Way, behold the retribution for sins and merits from incalculable kalpas past up to the present day, as clearly as observing a precious lapis lazuli gem in the palm of my hand, transparent inside and out, without any doubt."
Ānanda immediately stepped forward, adjusted his robes, prostrated, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this teaching be called as it is expounded?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Wheel of Transmigration through the Five Paths: The Retribution of Sin and Merit.

If there are good men or good women who recite and propagate it, their merit shall be immeasurable; they shall behold and serve the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, shall not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions, and shall attain the concentration of non-perception."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, five hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
At that time, the assembly of devas, nāgas, and spirits beneath the tree, as well as twelve thousand faithful laymen and six thousand faithful laywomen, all entered upon the tracks of the Path.
They all came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
This concludes the *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit* spoken by the Buddha.
